description: Eye contact, facial expressions, gestures, positioning and body language — and the active listening behaviours (open posture, nodding, reflecting, summarising) that show service users they are heard.
content_html:
What We Say Without Words

Research consistently shows that a significant proportion of how a message lands comes not from the words spoken but from non-verbal communication: the look on a practitioner's face, the way they position their body, whether they make eye contact or glance away. In a health or social care setting, non-verbal signals can either reinforce or completely contradict the verbal message. A care worker who says “take as much time as you need” while visibly checking their watch sends two opposite messages. Service users, particularly those who are anxious or in pain, read these signals carefully.

Consider Blessing, a support worker at a residential home for adults with acquired brain injuries. She is speaking with Kevin, a 43-year-old resident who is frustrated about a change to his medication schedule. Kevin has difficulty forming sentences quickly; Blessing needs every element of her non-verbal communication to signal that she is fully present. This lesson maps out exactly what that looks like — and what to avoid.

Eye Contact and Facial Expressions

Appropriate eye contact tells a service user: “I am focused on you.” It is not a fixed stare — that can feel intimidating — but a warm, steady gaze that the practitioner maintains for most of a conversation, looking away naturally from time to time. For Kevin, Blessing maintains eye contact while he is searching for words. She does not look at the door, her phone or the medication chart. This communicates patience and respect without her needing to say a word.

Facial expressions must match the tone of the conversation. If Kevin expresses frustration, Blessing's face shows she understands — a slight nod, a concerned expression. If she were to smile blankly while he described his distress, he would feel dismissed. Consistent, genuine facial expressions build trust; inconsistent ones confuse and unsettle service users.

Key Fact

The non-verbal communication skills listed in the spec are: adapting type/method to needs; eye contact; facial expressions; gestures; positioning (including space, height and personal space); positive body language (no crossed arms/legs); and sense of humour.

Gestures, Positioning and Space

Gestures such as a gentle nod, an open palm or a reassuring hand gesture (where culturally appropriate and with consent) can reinforce what is being said. They also support communication with service users who have limited speech. Overuse of gestures, or gestures that feel exaggerated or theatrical, can feel condescending.

Positioning covers three interconnected ideas: space, height and personal space. Blessing sits at the same level as Kevin rather than standing over him. Being at a similar height removes a power imbalance — a practitioner looming over a seated resident in a wheelchair signals authority, not partnership. She also considers the distance between them: close enough to communicate warmth and attentiveness, but not so close as to invade his personal space, which could make Kevin feel uncomfortable or threatened.

Positive Body Language

Positive body language means an open, relaxed stance. The spec specifically mentions no crossed arms or legs. Crossing the arms can suggest defensiveness or impatience even when the practitioner does not intend it. Blessing faces Kevin directly, her hands resting in her lap, her body turned toward him. This open posture sends a message that she is not in a hurry and has no barriers between them. Sense of humour, used appropriately, can also reduce tension — a light-hearted comment at the right moment can ease anxiety and help a service user feel more at ease. It should never be used to deflect a serious concern, but in the right context it humanises the interaction.

Students often write that active listening means “paying attention” or “listening carefully.” This is not enough for the exam. The spec names six specific behaviours that make up active listening: open relaxed posture; eye contact and looking interested; nodding agreement; showing empathy by reflecting feelings; clarifying; and summarising key points. A 6-mark question on active listening expects multiple named behaviours, each linked to a benefit for the service user. “Listening carefully” alone will score at most one mark.

Active Listening Skills

Active listening is a set of six named skills, not a passive state. The first two are physical: maintaining an open, relaxed posture and making eye contact while looking interested — these have already been covered above as part of non-verbal communication, but they are also the foundation of active listening. The next two involve responding: nodding to show agreement or acknowledgement, and showing empathy by reflecting feelings. When Kevin says “I feel like nobody tells me anything about my own care,” Blessing reflects: “It sounds like you're feeling left out of decisions that affect you.” This is not agreeing — it is showing she has heard and understood.

The final two active listening skills are clarifying and summarising. Clarifying means asking a question when something is unclear: “Could you tell me more about when you noticed this change?” This shows the listener is engaged, not just waiting for their turn to speak. Summarising at the end of a conversation — “So, if I've understood correctly, you're concerned about the new timing, and you'd like to discuss it with the nurse” — confirms the key points, prevents misunderstanding, and shows the service user their concerns have been heard and will be acted on.

Key Fact

The six active listening skills are: (1) open relaxed posture; (2) eye contact, looking interested; (3) nodding agreement; (4) showing empathy, reflecting feelings; (5) clarifying; (6) summarising to show understanding of key points. All six are tested — knowing four of six is not enough for the top mark band.

Together, non-verbal communication and active listening skills help service users: feel valued and respected; trust the practitioner; feel confident expressing concerns and needs; understand that their input genuinely shapes their care; and experience less anxiety in unfamiliar care settings. For practitioners, using these skills consistently means more accurate information gathering, fewer misunderstandings, and care that is genuinely person-centred. Active listening is particularly powerful in settings where verbal communication is limited — for a service user with dementia, or a child who cannot articulate distress clearly, non-verbal signals from the practitioner communicate that they are safe and that their experience matters.
exam_tip_html: On a 6-mark Explain question about active listening, the most common error is writing “the practitioner listens carefully” or “they pay attention” as a complete answer. These phrases earn almost nothing. You must name specific active listening behaviours — open posture, eye contact, nodding, reflecting feelings, clarifying, summarising — and for each one explain WHY it matters for the service user in the named scenario. The OCR command word ‘Explain’ requires reasons: use ‘because’, ‘therefore’ or ‘this means that’ in every point. For example: “Blessing maintains eye contact (named behaviour) because this signals to Kevin that she is focused on him, therefore he feels his concerns are being taken seriously and is more likely to fully explain the problem (benefit).” Two or three such developed points, anchored to the named service user, will reach the Secure to Mastering band.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Non-verbal communication skills include eye contact, facial expressions, gestures, positioning (space, height, personal space), positive body language (no crossed arms) and appropriate use of humour — all must be adapted to the service user's needs and the situation.
  • Active listening is a set of six specific behaviours: open relaxed posture; eye contact and looking interested; nodding agreement; showing empathy and reflecting feelings; clarifying; and summarising key points. It is not simply ‘paying attention’.
  • Together, these skills help service users feel valued, respected and understood, build trust, and ensure that the practitioner receives accurate information — all of which contribute directly to person-centred care.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is one of the six active listening skills named in the spec?
A) Using appropriate vocabulary
B) Adjusting volume
C) Summarising key points
D) Using medical jargon
Identify one non-verbal communication skill a practitioner should use when speaking with a service user.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any correct non-verbal skill. Accept: eye contact; facial expressions; gestures; positioning (space/height/personal space); positive body language/no crossed arms; sense of humour. Do not accept verbal skills such as tone or pace.

practice_questions.text: Outline what is meant by 'reflecting feelings' as an active listening skill.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic description (e.g. repeating or acknowledging what the service user has said about their feelings); 1 mark for development or example (e.g. by saying back to the service user what they appear to be feeling, such as 'it sounds like you are worried about your appointment', the practitioner shows they have understood and encourages the service user to continue).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a practitioner in a walk-in centre should use eye contact and positioning when speaking with a service user who is anxious about a minor procedure.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per skill). Eye contact (up to 2): describes appropriate use (1) — e.g. maintains a warm, steady eye contact rather than looking away or checking notes; development (1) — this shows the service user the practitioner is focused on them, which reduces anxiety and helps the service user feel their concerns are being taken seriously. Positioning (up to 2): describes appropriate positioning (1) — e.g. sits at the same level/height as the service user, at a comfortable distance that respects personal space; development (1) — being at the same height removes the sense of a power imbalance and makes the service user feel equal and respected, which is particularly important for a service user who is already anxious. Both answers must be linked to the walk-in centre context or the service user's anxiety for full marks.

practice_questions.text:
Suki is a health care assistant at a 40-bed NHS hospital ward. She is speaking with Darnell, a 25-year-old patient who has been told he will need to stay in hospital for several days following a diagnosis of a serious infection. Darnell is distressed and struggling to explain his concerns clearly.

Explain how Suki could use active listening skills to support Darnell during this conversation.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Explains at least three specific active listening skills by name. Each skill linked with a reason (because/therefore/this means that) and anchored to Darnell's distress and the hospital setting. Example chains: 'Suki maintains an open, relaxed posture (skill) because crossed arms or a tense stance would signal she is uncomfortable or in a hurry; this means Darnell feels she is fully present and safe to speak' / 'Suki reflects Darnell's feelings — for example, saying “It sounds like you’re really worried about being away from home” (skill) because this shows she has heard and understood his emotional state; Darnell feels valued rather than dismissed, which encourages him to share the full picture of his concerns' / 'Suki summarises at the end of the conversation, reviewing the key points Darnell has raised (skill), which confirms she has understood correctly and prevents misunderstanding about what will happen next'. Judgement or conclusion not required for 6-mark, but expected for 8-mark.

Secure (3-4 marks): Two or more active listening skills named with explanation. Generally linked to Darnell or the hospital ward. Uses some connective language. Benefits identified.

Developing (1-2 marks): One active listening skill named, or general statements about listening without naming specific behaviours. Little connection to the named service user or setting.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which positive body language supports communication with a service user in a care setting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per way, up to 2 marks. Accept: no crossed arms means the service user does not interpret the posture as defensive or impatient (1); facing the service user with an open stance signals engagement and willingness to listen (1); using an appropriate sense of humour can reduce tension and make the service user feel more comfortable (1). Brief description of each — a named behaviour alone scores 1 mark; a named behaviour with a development or reason scores more securely.

knowledge_checks.q: How many specific active listening skills are named in the spec for this topic?
Which of the following is NOT one of the six active listening skills in the spec?
Maintaining an open, relaxed posture and making _____ contact are the first two active listening skills in the spec.
When a practitioner sits at the same _____ as a service user who is seated, they remove a potential power imbalance in the interaction.
Match each active listening skill to what it involves:
right: Describing back to the speaker what they appear to be feeling
Asking a question to check understanding of what was said
Reviewing key points to confirm shared understanding
A non-verbal signal that shows acknowledgement and agreement

flashcard_questions.a: Communication through body language, facial expressions, gestures, eye contact and positioning, not words.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the six active listening skills listed in the spec.
flashcard_questions.a: Open relaxed posture; eye contact/looking interested; nodding; reflecting feelings; clarifying; summarising.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is it important for a practitioner to maintain appropriate eye contact during a conversation?
flashcard_questions.a: It signals full attention and respect, helping the service user feel heard and valued.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'reflecting feelings' mean as an active listening skill?
flashcard_questions.a: Describing back to the service user what they appear to be feeling, to show understanding.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'clarifying' mean as an active listening skill?
flashcard_questions.a: Asking a question to check the listener has correctly understood what the speaker said.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 'summarising' mean as an active listening skill?
flashcard_questions.a: Briefly reviewing the main points to confirm shared understanding at the end of a conversation.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does the spec specify 'no crossed arms' as positive body language?
flashcard_questions.a: Crossed arms can signal defensiveness or impatience, even when the practitioner does not intend this.

flashcard_questions.q: How should a practitioner position themselves relative to a service user in a wheelchair?
flashcard_questions.a: At the same height, e.g. by sitting down, to remove the power imbalance of looming over them.

flashcard_questions.q: What is personal space in the context of non-verbal communication?
flashcard_questions.a: The physical space immediately around a person they regard as their own; entering it without consent causes discomfort.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between non-verbal communication and active listening?
flashcard_questions.a: Non-verbal covers body signals (posture, expressions, eye contact); active listening adds specific responsive behaviours (nodding, reflecting, clarifying, summarising).

flashcard_questions.q: Name two benefits for a service user when a practitioner uses active listening skills.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two: feels valued and respected; trusts the practitioner; feels safe to express concerns; receives accurate, person-centred care.

flashcard_questions.q: When is sense of humour an appropriate non-verbal/verbal communication tool in care?
flashcard_questions.a: When used lightly to ease tension in a low-stakes moment, never to deflect a serious concern.

glossary_terms.definition: Communication through body language, facial expressions, gestures, eye contact and positioning rather than through words.
A set of deliberate, observable behaviours a listener uses to show a speaker that they are fully engaged and understood.
The act of looking at a person's eyes during conversation, used to signal attention, interest and respect.
Describing back to a speaker the feelings or content of what they have said, to show understanding and encourage them to continue.
Asking a question or checking understanding to make sure the listener has correctly interpreted what the speaker has said.
Briefly reviewing the main points of a conversation to confirm shared understanding and show the listener has been attentive.
The physical space immediately surrounding a person that they regard as their own; entering it without consent can cause discomfort or distress.
Body positioning and movement that signals openness, engagement and willingness to communicate, such as an open posture with uncrossed arms.

hero_image_caption: Non-verbal signals — eye contact, posture, gestures — tell a service user whether they are truly being heard, before a word is spoken.
